•Numbat: agent detection and response for laptops and workstations. 52 rules, single go binary for macOS, linux and windows
•Bumblebee: read-only supply chain scanner for dev machines. covers packages, MCP configs, and editor and browser extensions. 

a lot more open source contributions coming soon!

quotedTweet.text:
Banger paper from Google Research on multi-agent proof discovery.

(bookmark it)

It's really interesting to see this emerging multi-agent pattern: not enforcing too much execution structure and pairing it with dedicated agents for advising and verification.

I think it is generally applicable as well. Great read.

Here is how it works:

Cogentic runs on Gemini and works on open problems in theoretical computer science, starting from the problem statement with no expert hints.

The system works in rounds, and the orchestrator decides how many provers to run in each round. Every prover gets one direction to work on, such as a specific bound or a counterexample search, plus a short briefing that a summarizer agent writes from earlier attempts and verifier feedback. Each summarizer writes its briefing independently, so provers in the same round read different summaries of the same history.

Each draft goes through two adversarial verifiers. One checks the draft on its own, and the other reads all of the round's drafts side by side to catch shared mistakes. A draft is accepted only if both pass it.

The agents share state through two disk documents. A record logs every attempt with the objection it failed on, and a ledger stores verified lemmas and ruled-out directions. An auditor extracts correct lemmas from rejected proofs, verifies them again independently, and adds them to the ledger.

A separate process advisor reads the verification logs across rounds and updates the instructions given to provers and verifiers. The orchestrator and the advisor can't give mathematical opinions, so the provers provide all the math.

It produced new results on five open problems in online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design, each checked by domain experts. Most problems took around 100 Gemini calls, and the hardest took around 1,000.

Paper: https://t.co/QdCVWgn54S

Chat with Paper: https://t.co/vJsdwneoQe
quotedTweet.translationZh:
Google Research 关于多 agent 证明发现的一篇重磅论文。

（建议收藏）

看到这种新兴的多 agent 模式真的很有意思：不过度强制执行结构，同时配备专门的建议和验证 agents。

我认为它也具有普遍适用性。非常值得一读。

它的工作方式如下：

Cogentic 基于 Gemini 运行，处理理论计算机科学中的开放问题，从问题陈述开始，不依赖专家提示。

系统按轮次运行，编排器决定每轮运行多少个证明器。每个证明器都会得到一个研究方向，例如某个具体边界或反例搜索，以及一份简短简报；简报由 summarizer agent 根据早期尝试和验证器反馈撰写。每个 summarizer 都独立撰写简报，所以同一轮中的证明器会读到同一段历史的不同摘要。

每份草稿都会经过两个对抗式验证器。一个单独检查草稿本身，另一个并排阅读该轮所有草稿，以捕捉共同错误。只有两个验证器都通过，草稿才会被接受。

这些 agents 通过两个磁盘文档共享状态。record 记录每次尝试及其失败时遇到的反对意见，ledger 存储已验证的引理和已排除的方向。auditor 会从被拒绝的证明中提取正确引理，再次独立验证，并加入 ledger。

一个独立的 process advisor 会跨轮次读取验证日志，并更新给证明器和验证器的指令。编排器和 advisor 不能给出数学意见，所以所有数学内容都由证明器提供。

它在 online learning、auction theory 和 mechanism design 的五个开放问题上产生了新结果，每个结果都经过领域专家检查。大多数问题大约需要 100 次 Gemini 调用，最难的问题大约需要 1,000 次。

posts.text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

editorial.rationale: 含可复用使用经验

posts.translationZh:
我们会花更多时间去理解语言模型的输出。几点想法和技巧：

写作。我试过一个很有效的方法：让你的 LLM 用 ASD-STE100 解释某个东西。它是一套最初为航空航天维护文档开发的受控语言规范。LLM 很熟悉这种语言，而且它对清晰写作风格有严格约束，我常常觉得这样更易读。有时我会稍微放宽一点，比如要求“达到 ASD-STE100 的 80%”，因为规范本身相当严格。但还有更好的方式：

图表 / 图像。不要让 LLM 写文字，而是让它创建图表。这些内容往往更容易处理、解析和理解。但还有更好的方式：

网页。要求输出“HTML”，得到一个漂亮、交互式的网页。LLM 在前端方面越来越强，可以创建漂亮的体验、动画等。但还有更好的方式：

讲解视频。我最看好的输出形式，是针对任意主题生成完全定制化的讲解视频。可以尝试类似这样的提示：“Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration”。（后者需要 API key，或者你可以让 LLM 帮你找一些能用本地算力运行的不错免费替代方案。）这真的开始可用了！

总结：
- 随着 LLM 变得更强，它们会自主完成越来越多的基础工作，而我们的许多工作会抽象到监督和理解层面。
- 幸运的是，LLM 在这里也能帮上忙，因为随着智能和代码变得越来越充裕，你可以要求生成大型、定制、可丢弃的软件制品（例如 Web 应用、讲解视频），这些东西以前根本不值得创建。多推动边界，你会感到惊讶。

posts.text:
Hi @RubenLaukkonen, you are an excellent scientist too (I especially like your work with @shamilch). But I strongly disagree with what you say here. Because  I respect your work, I will explain why.

My credence in consciousness for current LLMs being very close to zero (certainly >80% in the 'no consciousness' direction) is not a matter of faith, nor is it an argument from authority, nor is it "unscientific". It is a conclusion I reach based on years of research and conversation, and it is grounded in reason and evidence - the cornerstones of science. I know you aware of this work (e.g., the @BBSJournal collection along with 50 commentaries). 

I am not 'dictating' the probability of AI consciousness. I am expressing my rationally-held view. You may (and do) come to a different conclusion. That's fine. We can disagree on what credences are reasonable, but there's no need to mischaracterise.

Of course I might be wrong, and I always say that nobody can be 100% sure in either direction. I explicitly admit the possibility of being wrong in many places (e.g., the BBS paper), which is why even trying to build conscious AI is a terrible idea (something I have also been saying for years). I have also been clear what would change my credences (e.g., positive evidence for computational functionalism).

I do believe there are many dangers to taking seriously calls for AI welfare, and that these dangers are generally underestimated and under-discussed. I will continue to point these dangers out. Again you disagree, but it seems wrong to dismiss my view as "unscientific" (its actually not even wrong, since we talking about ethics here).

You also imply that my views are 'extremist' which I find disappointing. Many other scientists and philosophers share these views, some defending even stronger versions. As a matter of descriptive accuracy, it feels wrong to characterise all of us as 'extreme'. What's more, this term has political connotations which I do not think are helpful or appropriate given the febrile nature of this debate. 

My colleagues who hold different views from me (e.g., @jeffrsebo,  @rgblong, @camhberg) do so for their own good reasons, which I respect and engage with. Their views are also based on reason and evidence. I disagree with a lot of they say, but I do not dismiss them as being faith-based, arguing from authority, or being unscientific. They are none of these things. I am sure they have excellent intentions, and that they are doing their best to navigate this complicated situation. In fact we have a lot of common ground, which provides the basis for productive discussions. (See for example my response to @jeffrsebo from earlier today, where you will see lots of agreement: https://t.co/77kDb04jHI)

As for the religious leader business, I do think this is worth paying attention to. There are corporate incentives to having religious approval for a particular way of viewing AI, and I think it's naive to assume these interactions are simply an innocent 'sharing of honest views'.

All the best 🙏🏽

quotedTweet.text:
Hi @jeffrsebo - lots of respect for you too (& your colleagues like @camhberg & @rgblong), and a fair amount of common ground also. I doubt that @X is the best place to hash all this out, but I'll do my best to respond briefly.

Jeff (at the end): "I think Anil and I agree more than we disagree. But I also think that efforts to assess and address AI consciousness and welfare will be much more productive if they start from an acknowledgment of what makes it so important and so difficult."

I agree. The question of AI consciousness is of massive importance, and also massively difficult.

Jeff (at the start): "While the evidence for consciousness in current AI systems may be weak, the probability is already nonzero, plausibly non-negligible, and likely to increase over time, especially if and when AI systems acquire more biologically inspired architectures"

Agree. I have said many times that as AI gets more brainlike this could change credences. I do think there are good arguments why its not just a matter of architecture, since there are good arguments against computational functionalism.

Jeff: "While over-attributing consciousness and welfare to AI carries serious risks, so does under-attributing them, and it can be reasonable to explore interventions that mitigate both risks at the same time, in proportion to the probability and severity of each."

Again, I agree. I am glad people like you are looking into the under-attribution possibility.  The problem is that the interventions can pull in different directions. Interventions to guard against possible AI harm often reinforce the negative consequences of false positives (e.g., through loss of control guardrails). That said, we can all agree that people should not be deliberately "torturing" LLMs.

Jeff "Despite what David suggests in the linked thread, most people who support AI welfare work, including at Anthropic, are not certain that AI systems are or will be welfare subjects. They think this is a realistic possibility worthy of serious consideration"

I agree with this too, and the people I spoke with directly at @AnthropicAI have been impressively open and open minded.  This did not include the senior management, and the company has its own identity too.

Jeff "Despite what Anil suggests here, this debate is not a matter of neuroscience and philosophy on one side and "the techno-chambers of the frontier firms" on the other."

I mostly stand by this. I think it characterises the majority of the relevant dynamics. There are important exceptions (e.g., @mustafasuleyman at @MicrosoftAI). My point is that the majority of the frontier work on this topic concerns examining their own models, rather than supporting work trying to understand the necessary/sufficient conditions for consciousness where we know it exists. (In us.). Also, I did mean 'techo-chamber' - a neologism which probably won't catch on ;-)

Jeff "Serious scientists, philosophers, and AI developers are on both sides."

I agree, and didn't say otherwise.

Jeff: "Corporate incentives also cut both ways. In some contexts, companies may have an incentive to play up AI consciousness in order to hype capabilities and encourage engagement with their models. In other contexts, they may have an incentive to play it down in order to avoid calls for oversight and regulation, especially as welfare protections become costlier. In any case, even if incentives pushed in one direction, that would not settle whether AI systems are, in fact, conscious and deserving of protection."

Indeed, but I think it helps to consider the motivations in this larger context. As I wrote in my @NoemaMag piece, there is an emerging mythology about conscious AI, which has a long history and some disturbing undercurrents which could lead to a catastrophic undervaluing of human life and human consciousness. (https://t.co/LmSiQnT9Wh)

Jeff: "I disagree that openness to AI consciousness and welfare is "profoundly dehumanising." A major part of what makes humanity special is our capacity to care for others, and in a world that still contains factory farming, cultivating that capacity should be seen as profoundly humanizing, an expression of our better angels."

I agree that our capacity to care makes us special (if not unique, many other animals do this too),  that this capacity should be cultivated, and that factory farming should be stopped. But the cultivation should be in the most appropriate directions. If we end up caring too much about our AI agents, this can be dehumanizing in very literal ways: we diminish our view of ourselves as living, embodied human beings, we take ourselves further outside of nature (rather than recognising we are part of it), our ability to form relationships with other humans may suffer, and we may care less about our fellow sentient creatures, humans and beyond. In other words I mean dehumanizing in the literal sense of what humanism means. Here I am mostly aligned with @mustafasuleyman's 'Humanist AI' though I would add more nuance (https://t.co/uRGFGfzxez).

Jeff: "Granted, we can take this impulse too far, which is why we need serious research and policy to strike a balance. Still, the aim should be extending care appropriately, not dismissing the project altogether."

I do not want to dismiss it, and I'm glad you and others are working on it. But to me the right balance is not being struck. The fact that we don't know for sure does not mean that we know nothing. I will argue for my view, just as I expect you do for yours.  And as you say, we share much common ground 🙏🏽

(For anyone who has made it this far, the real meat of the debate - with views on all sides - can be found in this @BBSJournal collection, with my target article and response, and 50 commentaries from peers in academia, tech, and beyond - representing pretty much every perspective on this important issue.) https://t.co/Tsaslytu56

嗨 @jeffrsebo，我也非常尊重你（以及像 @camhberg 和 @rgblong 这样的同事），我们之间也有不少共同点。我怀疑 @X 不是把这些问题彻底谈清楚的最佳场所，但我会尽量简短回应。

Jeff（开头处）：“虽然当前 AI 系统具备意识的证据可能很弱，但其概率已经非零，可能不可忽视，并且很可能随着时间推移而增加，尤其是当 AI 系统获得更多受生物启发的架构时。”

Jeff：“尽管 David 在链接线程中有所暗示，但大多数支持 AI 福利工作的人，包括 Anthropic 的人，并不确定 AI 系统现在或未来会成为福利主体。他们认为这是一个现实可能性，值得认真考虑。”

这一点我也同意，我直接接触过的 @AnthropicAI 人员表现得非常开放，也很有开放心态。不过这不包括高层管理层，而且公司本身也有自己的身份认同。

Jeff：“尽管 Anil 在这里有所暗示，这场辩论并不是一边是神经科学和哲学，另一边是‘前沿公司的技术回音室’。”

我基本坚持这一点。我认为它描述了相关动态中的大部分情况。当然也有重要例外（例如 @MicrosoftAI 的 @mustafasuleyman）。我的意思是，前沿公司在这个话题上的大多数工作，关注的是检查它们自己的模型，而不是支持那些试图理解意识存在处（也就是我们身上）必要/充分条件的研究。另外，我确实写的是 'techo-chamber'，这是个大概不会流行起来的新词 ;-)

Jeff：“严肃的科学家、哲学家和 AI 开发者站在双方。”

我同意，也没有说过相反的话。

Jeff：“企业激励也会双向作用。在某些情况下，公司可能有动机夸大 AI 意识，以炒作能力并鼓励用户与模型互动。在另一些情况下，公司可能有动机淡化它，以避免监督和监管呼声，尤其是在福利保护变得更昂贵时。无论如何，即便激励朝一个方向推动，也不能决定 AI 系统事实上是否有意识、是否值得保护。”

确实如此，但我认为把这些动机放在更大的语境中考虑是有帮助的。正如我在 @NoemaMag 文章中写到的，一种关于有意识 AI 的神话正在兴起，它有着悠久历史，也有一些令人不安的暗流，可能导致对人类生命和人类意识的灾难性低估。（https://t.co/LmSiQnT9Wh）

Jeff：“我不同意说对 AI 意识和福利持开放态度是‘深刻去人性化’的。人类之所以特殊，一个重要部分在于我们关怀他者的能力；在一个仍然存在工厂化养殖的世界里，培养这种能力应被视为深刻的人性化，是我们更好天性的体现。”

我同意，我们的关怀能力让我们特殊（即便不唯一，许多其他动物也会如此），这种能力应该被培养，工厂化养殖也应该被停止。但培养应该朝最合适的方向进行。如果我们最终过度关心 AI agents，这可能以非常字面的方式去人性化：我们会弱化对自身作为有生命、具身人类的理解，把自己进一步置于自然之外（而不是认识到我们是自然的一部分），我们与其他人类建立关系的能力可能受损，我们也可能更少关心其他有感知的生命，包括人类以及人类之外的生命。换句话说，我所说的去人性化，是从人文主义含义出发的字面意义。在这一点上，我大体认同 @mustafasuleyman 的“Humanist AI”，不过我会加入更多细微差别（https://t.co/uRGFGfzxez）。

Jeff：“诚然，我们可能把这种冲动推得太远，这也是为什么我们需要严肃研究和政策来取得平衡。不过，目标应该是恰当地扩展关怀，而不是完全否定这个项目。”

我并不想否定它，我也很高兴你和其他人在做这项工作。但在我看来，目前并没有取得正确平衡。我们不能因为不知道确定答案，就等于什么都不知道。我会为自己的观点辩护，正如我期待你也会为你的观点辩护。正如你所说，我们有很多共同点 🙏🏽

I agree with this too, and the people I spoke with directly at @AnthropicAI have been impressively open and open minded.  This did not include the senior management, and the company has its own identity too.

Jeff "Despite what Anil suggests here, this debate is not a matter of neuroscience and philosophy on one side and "the techno-chambers of the frontier firms" on the other."

I mostly stand by this. I think it characterises the majority of the relevant dynamics. There are important exceptions (e.g., @mustafasuleyman at @MicrosoftAI). My point is that the majority of the frontier work on this topic concerns examining their own models, rather than supporting work trying to understand the necessary/sufficient conditions for consciousness where we know it exists. (In us.). Also, I did mean 'techo-chamber' - a neologism which probably won't catch on ;-)

Jeff "Serious scientists, philosophers, and AI developers are on both sides."

I agree, and didn't say otherwise.

Jeff: "Corporate incentives also cut both ways. In some contexts, companies may have an incentive to play up AI consciousness in order to hype capabilities and encourage engagement with their models. In other contexts, they may have an incentive to play it down in order to avoid calls for oversight and regulation, especially as welfare protections become costlier. In any case, even if incentives pushed in one direction, that would not settle whether AI systems are, in fact, conscious and deserving of protection."

Indeed, but I think it helps to consider the motivations in this larger context. As I wrote in my @NoemaMag piece, there is an emerging mythology about conscious AI, which has a long history and some disturbing undercurrents which could lead to a catastrophic undervaluing of human life and human consciousness. (https://t.co/LmSiQnT9Wh)

Jeff: "I disagree that openness to AI consciousness and welfare is "profoundly dehumanising." A major part of what makes humanity special is our capacity to care for others, and in a world that still contains factory farming, cultivating that capacity should be seen as profoundly humanizing, an expression of our better angels."

I agree that our capacity to care makes us special (if not unique, many other animals do this too),  that this capacity should be cultivated, and that factory farming should be stopped. But the cultivation should be in the most appropriate directions. If we end up caring too much about our AI agents, this can be dehumanizing in very literal ways: we diminish our view of ourselves as living, embodied human beings, we take ourselves further outside of nature (rather than recognising we are part of it), our ability to form relationships with other humans may suffer, and we may care less about our fellow sentient creatures, humans and beyond. In other words I mean dehumanizing in the literal sense of what humanism means. Here I am mostly aligned with @mustafasuleyman's 'Humanist AI' though I would add more nuance (https://t.co/uRGFGfzxez).

Jeff: "Granted, we can take this impulse too far, which is why we need serious research and policy to strike a balance. Still, the aim should be extending care appropriately, not dismissing the project altogether."

I do not want to dismiss it, and I'm glad you and others are working on it. But to me the right balance is not being struck. The fact that we don't know for sure does not mean that we know nothing. I will argue for my view, just as I expect you do for yours.  And as you say, we share much common ground 🙏🏽

(For anyone who has made it this far, the real meat of the debate - with views on all sides - can be found in this @BBSJournal collection, with my target article and response, and 50 commentaries from peers in academia, tech, and beyond - representing pretty much every perspective on this important issue.) https://t.co/Tsaslytu56

Thanks @RubenLaukkonen. One more response, and then I'll stop, I promise :-)

(i) The GDM paper in my mind provides a Bayesian method for assessing the sensitivity of credences to altering parameters. The credence ranges themselves should not be taken all that seriously. This was a point I made clearly in my suggested edits.

(ii) Relatedly, I do not assume I am correct. Instead, I try to give reasons why my arguments might stand up, and then explore the consequences *if* I am right. That is the relevant conditional.

(iii) Again relatedly, I am not sure what you mean when you say "huge swathes of scientists disagree with your starting point".  My starting point (e.g., in BBS) is that we don't know whether substrate-independent computation is sufficient for consciousness, and we don't know whether biological substrate properties are necessary.  I then try to give arguments against algorithmic sufficiency and in favour of (biological) substrate necessity.  (I think the former are currently stronger than the latter.) Many scientists may disagree with my conclusions (though a fair number agree), but the starting point seems fairly reasonable to me.

(iv) What counts as a substrate is a good question. Having discussed extensively with Shamil in the context of 'critical level' in GDM, I am persuaded that there is a minimum grain that could count as critical, even if the substrate properties that have most explanatory power involve multiple scales or cross-scale integration a la Milinkovic and Aru.

(v) My credence in current AI being conscious is indeed extremely close to zero, but it is not zero. I stand by this. Conventional p-value thresholds do not seem relevant here, since this is not a statistical test based on sampling of a distribution. My credence on normal apples falling up rather than down (on the surface of the earth, in normal circumstances) is nomologically zero.

(vi) Finally, I do not ignore the potential downsides of false negatives: even if I think they're highly unlikely, I could be wrong, and the downsides if so would be major. I attach the relevant passages from BBS (§6.1) . Having said this, given my near-zero credence in LLM consciousness, and given that plenty of other people are focusing on false negatives, I make no apology for emphasising the downsides of the false positives - these are also severe and far more likely IMO.

(vi) I'm glad we agree that current AI is unlikely to be conscious - common ground!

Thanks again

Hi @RubenLaukkonen, you are an excellent scientist too (I especially like your work with @shamilch). But I strongly disagree with what you say here. Because  I respect your work, I will explain why.

My credence in consciousness for current LLMs being very close to zero (certainly >80% in the 'no consciousness' direction) is not a matter of faith, nor is it an argument from authority, nor is it "unscientific". It is a conclusion I reach based on years of research and conversation, and it is grounded in reason and evidence - the cornerstones of science. I know you aware of this work (e.g., the @BBSJournal collection along with 50 commentaries). 

I am not 'dictating' the probability of AI consciousness. I am expressing my rationally-held view. You may (and do) come to a different conclusion. That's fine. We can disagree on what credences are reasonable, but there's no need to mischaracterise.

Of course I might be wrong, and I always say that nobody can be 100% sure in either direction. I explicitly admit the possibility of being wrong in many places (e.g., the BBS paper), which is why even trying to build conscious AI is a terrible idea (something I have also been saying for years). I have also been clear what would change my credences (e.g., positive evidence for computational functionalism).

I do believe there are many dangers to taking seriously calls for AI welfare, and that these dangers are generally underestimated and under-discussed. I will continue to point these dangers out. Again you disagree, but it seems wrong to dismiss my view as "unscientific" (its actually not even wrong, since we talking about ethics here).

You also imply that my views are 'extremist' which I find disappointing. Many other scientists and philosophers share these views, some defending even stronger versions. As a matter of descriptive accuracy, it feels wrong to characterise all of us as 'extreme'. What's more, this term has political connotations which I do not think are helpful or appropriate given the febrile nature of this debate. 

My colleagues who hold different views from me (e.g., @jeffrsebo,  @rgblong, @camhberg) do so for their own good reasons, which I respect and engage with. Jeff (at the end): "I think Anil and I agree more than we disagree. But I also think that efforts to assess and address AI consciousness and welfare will be much more productive if they start from an acknowledgment of what makes it so important and so difficult."

I agree. The question of AI consciousness is of massive importance, and also massively difficult.

Jeff (at the start): "While the evidence for consciousness in current AI systems may be weak, the probability is already nonzero, plausibly non-negligible, and likely to increase over time, especially if and when AI systems acquire more biologically inspired architectures"

Agree. I have said many times that as AI gets more brainlike this could change credences. I do think there are good arguments why its not just a matter of architecture, since there are good arguments against computational functionalism.

Jeff: "While over-attributing consciousness and welfare to AI carries serious risks, so does under-attributing them, and it can be reasonable to explore interventions that mitigate both risks at the same time, in proportion to the probability and severity of each."

Again, I agree. I am glad people like you are looking into the under-attribution possibility.  The problem is that the interventions can pull in different directions. Interventions to guard against possible AI harm often reinforce the negative consequences of false positives (e.g., through loss of control guardrails). That said, we can all agree that people should not be deliberately "torturing" LLMs.

Jeff "Despite what David suggests in the linked thread, most people who support AI welfare work, including at Anthropic, are not certain that AI systems are or will be welfare subjects. They think this is a realistic possibility worthy of serious consideration"

I agree with this too, and the people I spoke with directly at @AnthropicAI have been impressively open and open minded.  This did not include the senior management, and the company has its own identity too.

Jeff "Despite what Anil suggests here, this debate is not a matter of neuroscience and philosophy on one side and "the techno-chambers of the frontier firms" on the other."

I mostly stand by this. I think it characterises the majority of the relevant dynamics. There are important exceptions (e.g., @mustafasuleyman at @MicrosoftAI). My point is that the majority of the frontier work on this topic concerns examining their own models, rather than supporting work trying to understand the necessary/sufficient conditions for consciousness where we know it exists. (In us.). Also, I did mean 'techo-chamber' - a neologism which probably won't catch on ;-)

Jeff "Serious scientists, philosophers, and AI developers are on both sides."

I agree, and didn't say otherwise.

Jeff: "Corporate incentives also cut both ways. In some contexts, companies may have an incentive to play up AI consciousness in order to hype capabilities and encourage engagement with their models. In other contexts, they may have an incentive to play it down in order to avoid calls for oversight and regulation, especially as welfare protections become costlier. In any case, even if incentives pushed in one direction, that would not settle whether AI systems are, in fact, conscious and deserving of protection."

Indeed, but I think it helps to consider the motivations in this larger context. As I wrote in my @NoemaMag piece, there is an emerging mythology about conscious AI, which has a long history and some disturbing undercurrents which could lead to a catastrophic undervaluing of human life and human consciousness. (https://t.co/LmSiQnT9Wh)

Jeff: "I disagree that openness to AI consciousness and welfare is "profoundly dehumanising." A major part of what makes humanity special is our capacity to care for others, and in a world that still contains factory farming, cultivating that capacity should be seen as profoundly humanizing, an expression of our better angels."

I agree that our capacity to care makes us special (if not unique, many other animals do this too),  that this capacity should be cultivated, and that factory farming should be stopped. But the cultivation should be in the most appropriate directions. If we end up caring too much about our AI agents, this can be dehumanizing in very literal ways: we diminish our view of ourselves as living, embodied human beings, we take ourselves further outside of nature (rather than recognising we are part of it), our ability to form relationships with other humans may suffer, and we may care less about our fellow sentient creatures, humans and beyond. In other words I mean dehumanizing in the literal sense of what humanism means. Here I am mostly aligned with @mustafasuleyman's 'Humanist AI' though I would add more nuance (https://t.co/uRGFGfzxez).

Jeff: "Granted, we can take this impulse too far, which is why we need serious research and policy to strike a balance. Still, the aim should be extending care appropriately, not dismissing the project altogether."

I do not want to dismiss it, and I'm glad you and others are working on it. But to me the right balance is not being struck. The fact that we don't know for sure does not mean that we know nothing. I will argue for my view, just as I expect you do for yours.  And as you say, we share much common ground 🙏🏽

We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.
